He gathered all the camels in the train of his army that were carrying provisions and baggage, took off their burdens, and set men upon them equipped like cavalry. Having thus furnished them, he ordered them to go in front of the rest of the army toward the horsemen of Croesus; and after the camel-troop he commanded the infantry to follow; and behind the infantry he placed his whole force of cavalry. When all his men had been placed in their several positions, he charged them to spare none of the rest of the Lydians, slaying all who came in their way, but they were not to kill Croesus himself, not even if he should resist when he was captured. Such was his charge. He had set the camels opposite the horsemen for this reason: because the horse is afraid of the camel and cannot endure either to see its shape or to scent its smell. For this reason, then, the trick had been devised, in order that the cavalry of Croesus might be useless—the very force with which the Lydian king expected most to shine. And as they were coming together to battle, as soon as the horses scented the camels and saw them, they turned back, and the hopes of Croesus were at once brought to nothing. In those years the Medes often defeated the Lydians and the Lydians often defeated the Medes, and they fought, among other engagements, a battle by night. And as they still carried on the war with equally balanced fortune, in the sixth year a battle took place in which, when the fight had begun, it happened that day suddenly turned to night. This change of day Thales of Miletus had foretold to the Ionians, setting as its limit this very year in which the change took place. The Lydians and Medes, when they saw that night had come in place of day, ceased fighting and both became much more eager that peace should be made between them. These were the men who urged them to take the oaths, and they also arranged an exchange of marriages: they determined that Alyattes should give his daughter Aryenis to Astyages, son of Cyaxares, since without the compulsion of a strong tie agreements tend not to hold firmly together. There he was entertained as a guest by Croesus in the king's palace; and afterwards, on the third or fourth day, at Croesus's order, the servants led Solon around to see the royal treasuries, and they showed him everything — how great and magnificent it all was. After Solon had looked at it all and examined it at leisure, Croesus asked him, “My Athenian guest, much report of you has come to us, both of your wisdom and of your travels — how, in search of wisdom, you have visited many lands to see them. Now, then, a desire has come upon me to ask whether you have seen any man whom you consider the happiest of all men.” He asked this supposing that he himself was the happiest, but Solon, using no flattery and speaking only the truth, said, “Yes, O king — Tellus the Athenian.” Croesus, astonished at this, asked him earnestly, “In what way do you judge Tellus to be the happiest?” Solon replied, “Tellus, in the first place, lived when his native state was prospering, and he had sons who were fine and good, and saw children born to each of them and all of them growing up. And secondly, he had what with us passes for wealth, and he met with the most glorious end of his life: for when the Athenians fought a battle against their neighbors at Eleusis, he came up in support, routed the enemy, and there died a most noble death. The Athenians buried him publicly on the spot where he fell and honored him greatly.”

The Athenian Solon names as the happiest of men: he lived well, saw his children’s children, and died fighting at Eleusis and was buried where he fell.

## modern-en · cleobis · 31:0

After Solon had moved Croesus to ask further with his story about Tellus—recounting how many marks of happiness the man possessed—the king asked again whom he had judged worthy to be placed next after him, supposing that he himself would certainly win at least the second place. But Solon replied: “Cleobis and Biton. These men, Argives by birth, had wealth enough to live on and, in addition, bodily strength such as I shall describe. Both had equally won prizes in the games, and the following tale is also told of them. There was a festival of Hera among the Argives, and it was absolutely necessary that their mother should be carried in a cart to the temple. But the oxen were not brought up from the field in time. Barred by the shortage of time from any other solution, the young men put themselves under the yoke and drew the wagon, their mother riding upon it. So they pulled it for forty-five stades and arrived at the temple. After they had accomplished this and had been seen by the gathered crowd, a most excellent ending was given to their lives, and in this matter the deity showed that it is better for a man to die than to continue living. For the Argive men stood around praising the strength of the young men, and the Argive women praised the mother for having been lucky enough to bear such sons. The mother, overjoyed both by the deed itself and by the reports of it, took her stand before the image of the goddess and prayed that she would grant to her sons Cleobis and Biton, who had so greatly honored her, the gift that is best for a man to receive. After this prayer, once the young men had sacrificed and feasted, they lay down to sleep inside the temple itself and never rose again, but were held fast in that final ending. The Argives had statues made in their likeness and dedicated them as offerings at Delphi, believing that they had proved themselves most excellent men.”

One of two Argive brothers who pulled their mother’s ox-cart to the temple of Hera; she prayed for the best thing a man can have, and they died in their sleep.

## modern-en · peisistratus · 58:0

Of these two peoples, then, Croesus was informed that the Athenian was held in subjection and torn by faction under Peisistratus, son of Hippocrates, who was at that time tyrant of the Athenians. For to Hippocrates, while he was still a private citizen and had gone to view the Olympic games, a great marvel had occurred. After he had offered the sacrifice, the cauldrons standing upon the hearth, full of pieces of flesh and of water, boiled over without fire beneath them and ran over. Chilon the Lacedaemonian, who happened to be present and to have seen the marvel, advised Hippocrates first not to bring into his house a wife to bear him children, and secondly, if he already had one, to dismiss her, and, if he happened to have a son, to disown him. But Hippocrates, they say, was not willing to be persuaded by Chilon’s advice. And so afterward this Peisistratus was born to him. When the Athenians of the shore were at feud with those of the plain—Megacles, son of Alcmaeon, being leader of the first faction, and Lycurgus, son of Aristolaidas, leader of that of the plain—Peisistratus aimed at the tyranny for himself and gathered a third party. After he had collected supporters and proclaimed himself leader of the men of the mountain-lands, he contrived the following device: he inflicted wounds upon himself and upon his mules, and then drove his chariot into the market-place as if he had just escaped from his enemies, who, he alleged, had tried to kill him as he was driving into the country. He then begged of the commons that he might obtain some protection from them, for before this he had gained a reputation in his command against the Megarians, during which he took Nisaea and performed other signal services. The commons of the Athenians, being deceived, gave him a body of men chosen from among the dwellers in the city—men who became not the spearmen of Peisistratus but his club-men, for they followed behind him bearing wooden clubs. These rose up with Peisistratus and seized the Acropolis. Then Peisistratus became ruler of the Athenians, without disturbing the existing magistrates or changing the ancient laws; but he administered the State under that constitution which was already established, ordering it fairly and well.

Tyrant of Athens three times over: once by wounding himself and getting a bodyguard, once with a tall woman dressed as Athena riding into the city beside him, and once by force and mercenaries.

## modern-en · lygdamis · 60:0

Having thus recovered the tyranny in the manner described, Peisistratus, in accordance with the agreement he had made with Megacles, married the daughter of Megacles. But as he already had young sons, and as the descendants of Alcmaeon were said to be under a curse, he did not wish children to be born to him from his newly married wife, and so had intercourse with her in an unaccustomed manner. At first the woman kept this secret, but afterwards she told her mother—whether in answer to her inquiry or not I cannot say—and the mother told her husband Megacles. He then was deeply indignant at being dishonored by Peisistratus, and in his anger immediately moved to compose his quarrel with the men of his faction. When Peisistratus heard what was being done against him, he departed entirely from the land and came to Eretria, where he took counsel together with his sons. When the advice of Hippias prevailed—that they should try to win back the tyranny—they began to gather gifts of money from those states that owed them obligations for favors received. Many contributed great sums, but the Thebans surpassed the rest in the giving of money. Then, not to make the story long, time passed and at last everything was prepared for their return. For certain Argives came as mercenaries from the Peloponnesus, and a man of Naxos called Lygdamis had come to them of his own accord, showing very great zeal in providing both money and men.

The Naxian who gave Peisistratus money and men for his third return, and was set up as tyrant of Naxos for it.

Such was the condition of things that Croesus heard was prevailing among the Athenians during this time. As for the Lacedaemonians, he heard that they had escaped from great troubles and had now got the better of the Tegeans in the war. For while Leon and Hegesicles were kings of Sparta, the Lacedaemonians, who had been successful in all their other wars, suffered disaster only in the one they waged against the men of Tegea. Moreover, in earlier times they had had almost the worst laws of any Greeks, both in matters that concerned themselves alone and also in that they had no dealings with strangers. And they made their change to a good constitution of laws in this way: Lycurgus, a man of the Spartans who was held in high repute, came to the Oracle at Delphi, and as he entered the sanctuary of the temple the Pythian prophetess at once spoke as follows:

The lawgiver who gave Sparta its whole constitution — brought from Crete, or given by the Pythia, depending on who is telling it — and turned the worst-governed Greeks into the best.

## modern-en · anaxandrides · 66:0

In the earlier war, then, as I said, they struggled against the Tegeans continually with ill success; but in the time of Croesus, and in the reigns of Anaxandrides and Ariston at Lacedaemon, the Spartans had at last become victors in the war. And they became victors in the following manner: since they kept being defeated by the men of Tegea, they sent messengers to consult the Oracle at Delphi and asked what god they should propitiate in order to prevail over the men of Tegea in the war. The Pythian prophetess answered them that they should bring into their land the bones of Orestes, son of Agamemnon. But as they were not able to find the grave of Orestes, they sent men again to go to the god and ask about the place where Orestes lay. When the messengers who were sent asked this, the prophetess said as follows:

King of Sparta at the time of Croesus’s embassy.

## modern-en · othryades · 81:0

So in sending to his other allies, he sent also to Lacedaemon. But these—the Spartans, I mean—had at this very time (as it happened) a quarrel of their own in hand with the Argives about the district called Thyrea. For the Lacedaemonians had cut off this Thyrea, which was part of the Argive territory, and had taken it for themselves. At that time the Argives possessed the whole region toward the west extending as far down as Malea, both the parts on the mainland and also the island of Cythera with the other islands. When the Argives had come to the rescue to save their territory from being cut off, the two sides came to a parley and agreed that three hundred men should fight on each side, and whichever side had the better in the fight, that nation should possess the disputed land. They also agreed that the main body of each army should withdraw to its own country and not stand by while the contest was fought, for fear that, if the armies were present, one side, seeing their countrymen suffering defeat, would come up to their support. Having made this agreement, they withdrew, and chosen men of both sides were left behind and engaged in combat with one another. They fought and proved themselves evenly matched, and at last, of six hundred men, only three were left alive—on the Argive side Alcenor and Chromius, and on the Lacedaemonian side Othryades. These were left alive when night came on. The two Argives, supposing that they were the victors, set off to run back to Argos; but the Lacedaemonian Othryades, after stripping the corpses of the Argives and carrying their arms to his own camp, remained in his place. On the next day both sides came to the spot to inquire about the result, and for some time both claimed the victory for themselves: the one side saying that more of them had survived, the others declaring that those men had fled whereas their own man had stood his ground and had stripped the corpses of the other party. At length, because of this dispute, they fell upon one another and began to fight again, and after many had fallen on both sides, the Lacedaemonians were victorious. The Argives then cut their hair short, whereas formerly they were required by law to wear it long, and they made a law with a curse attached: that from that time forth no Argive man should grow his hair long nor their women wear ornaments of gold until they had won back Thyrea. The Lacedaemonians, on the contrary, laid down for themselves the opposite law: that they should wear long hair from that time forward, whereas before that time they had not worn it long. And they say that the one man left alive of the three hundred, Othryades, being ashamed to return to Sparta when all his comrades had been slain, killed himself there in Thyrea.

The one Spartan left standing after the Battle of the Champions at Thyrea, who stripped the Argive dead and stayed on the field — and afterwards killed himself for shame at outliving his three hundred.

## modern-en · thales · 73:0

After this, since Alyattes would not give up the Scythians when Cyaxares demanded them, war arose between the Lydians and the Medes that lasted five years. In those years the Medes often defeated the Lydians and the Lydians often defeated the Medes, and they fought, among other engagements, a battle by night. And as they still carried on the war with equally balanced fortune, in the sixth year a battle took place in which, when the fight had begun, it happened that day suddenly turned to night. This change of day Thales of Miletus had foretold to the Ionians, setting as its limit this very year in which the change took place. The Lydians and Medes, when they saw that night had come in place of day, ceased fighting and both became much more eager that peace should be made between them. Those who brought about the peace between them were Syennesis the Cilician and Labynetus the Babylonian. These were the men who urged them to take the oaths, and they also arranged an exchange of marriages: they determined that Alyattes should give his daughter Aryenis to Astyages, son of Cyaxares, since without the compulsion of a strong tie agreements tend not to hold firmly together. Now these nations observe the same ceremonies in the taking of oaths as the Greeks do, and in addition they make an incision in the skin of their arms and then lick up the blood, each from the other.

Thales of Miletus, who foretold the year of the eclipse that stopped the battle between the Medes and the Lydians, and who is said to have diverted the Halys so Croesus could cross.

But what do you think the islanders have been wishing and praying for ever since they heard that you were going to build ships against them, except to catch the Lydians at sea, so that they might take vengeance on you for the Hellenes on the mainland, whom you hold enslaved?” Croesus, they say, was greatly pleased with this reply, and, thinking the man had spoken well, he obeyed his suggestion and put a stop to the shipbuilding; and on that basis he formed a friendship with the Ionians who lived on the islands.

Bias of Priene, who talked Croesus out of building a fleet by telling him the islanders were buying horses — and who advised the Ionians, too late, to sail away and found one city in Sardinia.

And since Minos subdued much land and was fortunate in his fighting, the Carian nation was at that time by much the most famous of all nations, together with him. As evidence of this, they point to an ancient temple of Carian Zeus at Mylasa, in which the Mysians and Lydians share as brother races of the Carians, for they say that Lydos and Mysos were brothers of Car. ## modern-en · sarpedon · 172:0

The Lykians, however, have sprung originally from Crete (for in olden times the whole of Crete was possessed by barbarians). When the sons of Europa, Sarpedon and Minos, came to be at variance in Crete about the kingdom, Minos, having got the better in the strife of parties, drove out both Sarpedon himself and those of his party. They, having been expelled, came to the land of Milyas in Asia, for the land which the Lykians now inhabit was anciently called Milyas, and the Milyans were then called Solymoi. While Sarpedon reigned over them, they were called by the name they had when they came there, by which the Lykians are even now called by the neighboring tribes, namely Termilai. But when Lycos the son of Pandion came from Athens to the land of the Termilai and to Sarpedon — having himself been driven out by his brother Aigeus — then by the name taken from Lycos they were after a time called Lykians. The customs they have are partly Cretan and partly Carian; but one custom they have which is peculiar to them and in which they agree with no other people: they call themselves by their mothers and not by their fathers. If one asks his neighbor who he is, he will state his parentage on the mother's side and enumerate his mother's female ancestors. And if a woman who is a citizen marries a slave, the children are accounted of gentle birth; but if a man who is a citizen, though he were the first among them, has a slave for wife or concubine, the children are without civil rights.

Minos’s brother, driven out of Crete, who led the Termilai into the land that became Lycia.

This, the Persians say, is how Io came to Egypt — though the Hellenes tell it differently — and this, according to them, was the first injury. Afterwards, they say, some Hellenes (whose nationality they cannot name) put in at the Phoenician city of Tyre and carried off the king's daughter Europa. These must have been Cretans, and so the two sides were even. But after this, they say, the Hellenes committed the second wrong. They sailed in a warship to Aia in Colchis and up the river Phasis, and after completing the other business that had brought them there, they carried off the king's daughter Medea. The king of Colchis sent a herald to Hellas demanding satisfaction for the abduction and the return of his daughter. The Hellenes replied that since the barbarians had given no satisfaction for the abduction of Io the Argive, they would give none for Medea either.

The king’s daughter carried off from Tyre — the second of the four abductions with which Herodotus opens the quarrel between Europe and Asia.

## modern-en · io · 1:0

The learned among the Persians say the Phoenicians were the ones who started the quarrel. They came, so the story goes, from what is called the Erythraean Sea to the Mediterranean, and once they had settled in the land where they still live today, they immediately began making long sea voyages. Carrying Egyptian and Assyrian merchandise, they traded in many places, and eventually reached Argos — which at that time was the leading state in what is now called Hellas. When the Phoenicians arrived at Argos, they began selling their cargo. On the fifth or sixth day, when nearly all their goods had been sold, a great crowd of women came down to the shore, and among them was the king's daughter, whose name, as the Hellenes also agree, was Io, daughter of Inachus. The women were standing near the ship's stern, buying whatever pleased them most, when the Phoenicians, passing the word among themselves, suddenly rushed at them. Most of the women escaped by running, but Io and a few others were seized, thrown aboard the ship, and carried off at once to Egypt.

Daughter of Inachus, carried off from Argos by Phoenician traders — the first abduction, and the beginning of the whole business.

## modern-en · helen · 3:0

In the next generation, the Persians say, Alexander, the son of Priam, heard of these events and wanted to get a wife for himself out of Hellas by force, certain that he would never be required to give satisfaction, since the Hellenes had given none themselves. Barred by the shortage of time from any other solution, the young men put themselves under the yoke and drew the wagon, their mother riding upon it. So they pulled it for forty-five stades and arrived at the temple. After they had accomplished this and had been seen by the gathered crowd, a most excellent ending was given to their lives, and in this matter the deity showed that it is better for a man to die than to continue living. For the Argive men stood around praising the strength of the young men, and the Argive women praised the mother for having been lucky enough to bear such sons. The mother, overjoyed both by the deed itself and by the reports of it, took her stand before the image of the goddess and prayed that she would grant to her sons Cleobis and Biton, who had so greatly honored her, the gift that is best for a man to receive. After this prayer, once the young men had sacrificed and feasted, they lay down to sleep inside the temple itself and never rose again, but were held fast in that final ending. The Egyptians call the one on the north side Summer, and the one on the south side Winter; to Summer they pay reverence and make offerings, while to Winter they do the opposite. (a) This king, they said, gained great wealth in silver, more than any king born after him could match or even approach. Wishing to keep his treasure safe, he had a stone chamber built, with one of its walls forming part of the outside of his palace. The builder, however, had a design upon it, and he contrived as follows: he set one of the stones in such a way that it could easily be removed from the wall by two men, or even by a single man. So when the chamber was finished and the king stored his money inside it, the builder, after some time, drawing near the end of his life, called his two sons to him. He told them how he had arranged the matter when building the king's treasury, all in forethought for them, so that they might have ample means of living. He gave them the precise measurements for removing the stone, telling them that if they paid heed to this, they would be the stewards of the king's treasury. Then he died, and his sons made no long delay in setting to work. They went to the palace by night, found the stone in the wall of the chamber, dealt with it easily, and carried away a great quantity of the wealth within. (b) When the king happened to open the chamber, he was astonished to see the vessels falling short of their full amount, and he did not know whom to blame, since the seals were unbroken and the chamber had been shut close. But when, on opening the chamber a second time and a third, the money was each time seen to be diminished — for the thieves did not slacken in their assaults — he did as follows. He had traps made and set them around the vessels in which the money was kept; and when the thieves came as before and one of them entered, as soon as he came near a vessel he was caught fast in the trap. Realizing how desperate his case was, he immediately called his brother, showed him what had happened, and bade him climb in as quickly as possible and cut off his head, lest he be seen and recognized, bringing destruction upon his brother as well. To the other this seemed sound advice, and he was persuaded; he did so, and fitting the stone back into its place, he departed home carrying his brother's head with him. (c) When day came, the king entered the chamber and was utterly amazed to see the body of the thief held in the trap without its head, the chamber unbroken, and no way to come in or go out. Being at a loss, he hung the dead body up on the wall and set guards there, with orders to seize anyone seen weeping or lamenting and bring him before the king. When the body had been hung up, the mother was deeply grieved. Speaking with her surviving son, she ordered him to contrive, by whatever means he could, to take down and bring home the body of his dead brother; and if he failed to do this, she earnestly threatened that she would go and inform the king that he had the money. (d) Since the mother dealt harshly with the surviving son, and he could not persuade her with his many arguments, he contrived a device for his purpose. He provided himself with asses, filled some skins with wine, loaded them upon the asses, and drove them along. When he came opposite to those guarding the corpse, he pulled out two or three of the necks of the skins and loosened the cords with which they were tied. As the wine ran out, he began to beat his head and cry out loudly, as if he did not know which of the asses to turn to first. When the guards saw the wine flowing out in streams, they ran together onto the road with drinking vessels in their hands and collected the wine that was spilling, counting it pure gain. He railed at them all violently, pretending to be angry, and when the guards tried to appease him, after a while he feigned to be pacified and to abate his anger. At last he drove his asses out of the road and began to set their loads right. Then more talk arose among them, one or two of them made jokes at him and brought him to laugh with them, and in the end he made them a present of one of the skins as well. At that they lay down then and there without further ado, intending to drink, and they took him into their company and invited him to stay with them and join them in their drinking. So he, as one might expect, was persuaded and stayed. As they welcomed him in friendly fashion as they drank, he made them a present of another skin. So at length, having drunk liberally, the guards became completely drunk, and being overcome by sleep they went to bed on the very spot where they had been drinking. He then, since it was now far on in the night, first took down the body of his brother, and then in mockery shaved the right cheeks of all the guards. After that he placed the dead body upon the asses and drove them home, having accomplished what his mother had enjoined upon him. (e) When it was reported to the king that the dead body of the thief had been stolen away, he displayed great anger; and desiring above all to find out who it could be that devised these things, he did this — so at least they said, though I do not believe the account. He caused his own daughter to sit in a brothel and ordered her to receive all comers equally, and before lying with any of them she was to compel each one to tell her what was the most cunning and the most unholy deed he had done in all his life; and whoever should relate what had happened concerning the thief, she must seize him and not let him go. So she did as her father had enjoined. The thief, hearing the purpose for which this was done and wishing to outdo the king in cleverness, did this. From the body of one lately dead he cut off the arm at the shoulder and went with it under his cloak. Having gone in to the king's daughter and being asked the same question as the others, he related that he had done the most unholy deed when he cut off the head of his brother caught in a trap in the king's treasure-chamber, and the most cunning deed when he made the guards drunk and took down the dead body of his brother that had been hung up. When she heard this and tried to lay hold of him, the thief held out to her in the darkness the arm of the corpse, which she grasped and held, thinking she was holding the man's own arm. But the thief left it in her hands and departed, escaping through the door. (f) When this also was reported to the king, he was at first amazed at the ready invention and daring of the fellow. Then afterwards he sent round to all the cities and made proclamation, granting a free pardon to the thief and promising a great reward as well if he would come into his presence. The thief, trusting to the proclamation, came to the king, and Rhampsinitos marvelled greatly at him and gave him this daughter of his to wife, considering him to be the most knowing of all men. For just as the Egyptians were distinguished from all other men, so was he distinguished from the other Egyptians.

The rich king whose treasury a mason’s two sons robbed through a movable stone — the best story in Book 2 — and who ended by marrying his daughter to the thief.

## modern-en · cheops · 339:0

Down to the time when Rhampsinitos was king, they told me, there was nothing in Egypt but orderly rule, and Egypt prospered greatly. But after him Cheops became king and brought them to every kind of misery. He shut up all the temples, and having first stopped them from sacrificing there, he then ordered all the Egyptians to work for him. Some were assigned to drag stones from the quarries in the Arabian mountains to the Nile; others he ordered to receive the stones after they had been ferried across the river in boats, and to haul them to the so-called Libyan mountains. They worked in shifts of a hundred thousand men at a time, for three months straight. Ten years of this oppression passed while the causeway was built along which they hauled the stones — a causeway that is, in my view, a work not much less than the pyramid itself. Its length is five furlongs, its breadth ten fathoms, and its height, where it is highest, eight fathoms, and it is made of smoothed stone with figures carved upon it. For this, they said, the ten years were spent, as well as for the underground chambers on the hill on which the pyramids stand, which he had made as burial chambers for himself on an island, having led a channel from the Nile to the place. For the construction of the pyramid itself a period of twenty years passed. The pyramid is square, each side measuring eight hundred feet, and its height is the same. It is built of smoothed stones fitted together in the most perfect manner, not one of the stones being less than thirty feet in length.

The king who shut the temples, set the whole people to work on his pyramid for twenty years, and sold his own daughter’s favours to pay for it.

## modern-en · chephren · 342:0

This Cheops, the Egyptians said, reigned for fifty years; and after he died, his brother Chephren succeeded to the kingdom. This king followed the same pattern as the other in every respect, including the fact that he built a pyramid. His pyramid did not reach the dimensions of the one built by his predecessor — I know this, having measured it myself — and moreover it has no underground chambers beneath it, nor does a channel from the Nile flow to it as to the other, where the water coming through a built conduit flows around an island within, and where they say Cheops himself is buried. But for a foundation he laid the first course in Ethiopian stone of varied colors. He built this pyramid forty feet lower than the other in size, placing it next to the great pyramid. The two stand on the same hill, which is about a hundred feet high. And Chephren, they said, reigned fifty-six years.

Cheops’s brother and successor, who ruled in the same manner for fifty-six years; the Egyptians will not willingly say either brother’s name.

## modern-en · mykerinos · 344:0

After him, they said, Mykerinos became king over Egypt — the son of Cheops. His father's deeds displeased him, and he both opened the temples and gave the people, who had been ground down to the last extremity of misery, their liberty to return to their own affairs and to their sacrifices. He also handed down judgments in their lawsuits that were more just than those of all the other kings. For this reason the Egyptians praise this king above all the kings who had arisen in Egypt before him; for he not only gave good decisions, but also, when a man complained of a decision, he paid him compensation out of his own property and so satisfied his desire. But while Mykerinos was acting mercifully to his subjects and conducting himself in the way I have described, calamities befell him. The first was this: his daughter died, the only child he had in his house. Grieved beyond measure by what had happened, and wishing to bury his daughter in a more remarkable manner than others, he made a cow of wood, covered it over with gold, and then buried within it this daughter who, as I said, had died.

Cheops’s son, who opened the temples again and gave the people back their lives — and was told by the oracle that he had six years to live because Egypt was meant to suffer a hundred and fifty. He answered by lighting lamps and living the nights as well.

## modern-en · asychis · 351:0

After Mykerinos, the priests said, Asychis became king of Egypt, and he built for Hephaistos the temple gateway that faces the sunrise — by far the most beautiful and largest of the gateways. While all of them have figures carved upon them and countless other architectural ornaments, this one has them far more than the rest. In this king's reign, they told me, as the circulation of money was very slow, a law was passed for the Egyptians allowing a man to borrow the money he needed by offering as security the dead body of his father. An additional clause was added: the lender was to have a claim on the whole burial chamber belonging to the borrower, and the borrower who offered this security, if he refused to repay the debt, would be subject to this penalty — that neither he himself would be allowed burial when he died, either in the family tomb or any other, nor would he be allowed to bury any kinsman who died. Wishing to surpass the kings of Egypt before him, this king left as his memorial a pyramid that he made of bricks, on which there is an inscription carved in stone that says: “Do not despise me in comparison with the pyramids of stone, for I surpass them as much as Zeus surpasses the other gods. For with a pole they struck into the lake, and whatever mud stuck to the pole, they gathered up and made into bricks, and in this way they finished me.”

The king who made a law that a man might borrow on his father’s corpse, and built a pyramid of brick with an inscription telling it not to compare itself with the stone ones.

## modern-en · anysis · 352:0

and after him reigned a blind man from the city of Anysis, whose name was Anysis. In his reign the Ethiopians, led by their king Sabacos, marched against Egypt with a great host. So this blind man fled and took refuge in the marshlands, and the Ethiopian ruled over Egypt for fifty years, during which he did the following: whenever an Egyptian committed a transgression, he would never put him to death, but he sentenced each man according to the gravity of the offense, ordering them to throw up an embankment before the city each offender came from. In this way the cities were raised still higher than before; for they had first been embanked by those who dug the channels in the reign of Sesostris, and then again in the reign of the Ethiopian, and so they were raised very high. While other cities in Egypt also stood high, I think it was at Bubastis in particular that the earth was piled up most. In this city there is a temple very much worth mentioning, for though there are other larger and more costly temples, none is more pleasing to the eye than this one. Now Bubastis in the Greek tongue is Artemis,

The blind king of the city of the same name, who fled into the marshes when the Ethiopians came and hid there fifty years on a floating island of ash and earth.

## modern-en · sethos · 356:0

After him the priest of Hephaistos, whose name was Sethos, came to the throne. This man, they said, neglected and held in no regard the warrior class of the Egyptians, thinking he would have no need of them. Besides other slights he put upon them, he also took from them the plots of grain-land which had been granted to them as a special gift in the reigns of previous kings — twelve plots to each man. After this, Sanacharib, king of the Arabians and Assyrians, marched a great army against Egypt. Then the warriors of the Egyptians refused to come to the rescue, and the priest, being driven into a tight corner, entered the sanctuary of the temple and lamented before the image of the god the danger hanging over him. As he was lamenting, sleep came over him, and in his vision it seemed that the god came and stood beside him and encouraged him, saying he would suffer no harm if he went out to meet the army of the Arabians, for he himself would send him helpers. Trusting in what he had seen in his sleep, he took with him, they said, those Egyptians who were willing to follow, and encamped at Pelusion, for that was the route of the invasion. Not one of the warrior class followed him, but shopkeepers, artisans, and men of the marketplace. Then, after they arrived, field mice swarmed by night upon their enemies and ate through their quivers and their bows, and moreover the handgrips of their shields, so that the next day they fled, and being without weapons to defend themselves, great numbers of them fell. To this day this king stands in the temple of Hephaistos in stone, holding a mouse on his hand, and by letters inscribed he says these words: “Let whoever looks upon me learn to fear the gods.”

The priest of Hephaistos who despised the warrior class and was saved from Sennacherib by field-mice that ate the Assyrians’ bowstrings overnight.

## modern-en · psammetichos · 104:0

From there they went on to invade Egypt; and when they were in Syria, which is called Palestine, Psammetichus, king of Egypt, met them, and by gifts and entreaties he turned them from their purpose so that they should advance no further. As they retreated, when they came to the city of Ascalon in Syria, most of the Scythians passed through without doing any damage, but a few of them who had stayed behind plundered the temple of Aphrodite Urania. This temple, as I find by inquiry, is the most ancient of all the temples that belong to this goddess; for the temple in Cyprus was founded from this one, as the people of Cyprus themselves report, and it was the Phoenicians who founded the temple in Cythera, coming from this land of Syria. So these Scythians who had plundered the temple at Ascalon, and their descendants forever after, were smitten by the divinity with a disease that made them women instead of men. The Scythians say that for this reason they were diseased, and that for this reason travelers who visit Scythia today see among them the affliction of those whom the Scythians call Enareis.

One of the twelve kings, driven out and returned with the bronze men the oracle promised; he reunited Egypt, opened it to Greek traders, and shut two children away with a mute shepherd to find out which language came first. The two editions spell him Psammetichos and Psammetichus.

## modern-en · necos · 367:0

This Psammetichos had previously been a fugitive from the Ethiopian Sabacos, who had killed his father Necos; from him, I say, he had been a fugitive in Syria. When the Ethiopian departed as a result of the vision in the dream, the Egyptians of the district of Saïs brought him back to his own country. Afterwards, when he was king, it was his fate to be a fugitive a second time on account of the helmet, being driven by the eleven kings into the marshland. Holding that he had been gravely wronged by them, he considered how he might take vengeance on those who had driven him out. When he sent to the oracle of Leto in the city of Buto, where the Egyptians have their most truthful oracle, he was given the reply that vengeance would come when men of bronze appeared from the sea. He was strongly inclined not to believe that bronze men would come to help him; but not long afterwards, certain Ionians and Carians who had sailed out for plunder were forced to come ashore in Egypt, and having landed and being clad in bronze armor, one of the Egyptians, never having seen men in bronze armor before, came to the marshland and brought word to Psammetichos that bronze men had come from the sea and were plundering the plain. He, perceiving that the saying of the oracle was coming to pass, dealt in a friendly manner with the Ionians and Carians, and with large promises persuaded them to take his side. Then, having persuaded them, with the help of the Egyptians who favored his cause and of these foreign mercenaries, he overthrew the kings.

Psammetichos’s son, who began the canal to the Red Sea, gave it up when the oracle warned him, and sent Phoenicians to sail round Libya. The older translation spells him Necos; he is also the father Sabacos killed.

## modern-en · psammis · 374:0

After abandoning the canal, Necos turned to warfare. He had triremes built, some for the Mediterranean and some for the Arabian Gulf on the Red Sea. Their ship sheds can still be seen. He used these ships when he needed them. On land, Necos fought and defeated the Syrians at Magdolos. After the battle, he captured the great Syrian city of Cadytis. He dedicated the clothes he wore during these victories to Apollo, sending them to the temple of the Branchidai near Miletos. After a total reign of sixteen years, Necos died and passed the throne to his son Psammis.

Necos’s son, who reigned six years, invaded Ethiopia, and gave the Eleians the obvious answer about their own games.

## modern-en · apries · 376:0

When Psammis had been king of Egypt for only six years and had made an expedition to Ethiopia, and immediately afterwards ended his life, Apries son of Psammis inherited the kingdom in succession. This man came to be the most prosperous of all the kings up to that time, except only his forefather Psammetichos, and he reigned twenty-five years, during which he led an army against Sidon and fought a sea-battle with the king of Tyre. Since, however, it was fated that evil should come upon him, it came through a matter which I shall relate at greater length in the Libyan history, and only briefly here. Apries sent a great expedition against the Kyrenians and met with a correspondingly great disaster; and the Egyptians, considering him to blame for this, revolted against him, supposing that Apries had deliberately sent them out to obvious ruin so that — as they said — there might be a slaughter of them and he might the more securely rule over the rest of the Egyptians. Indignant at this, both the men who had returned from the expedition and the friends of those who had perished openly revolted.

Psammis’s son, the most prosperous king but one until his army went over to Amasis; he was kept alive in his own palace and then handed to the Egyptians, who strangled him.

## modern-en · patarbemis · 377:0

Hearing of this, Apries sent Amasis to them to put a stop to it by persuasion; and when he had come and was trying to restrain the Egyptians, as he was speaking and telling them not to revolt, one of the Egyptians stood up behind him and placed a helmet on his head, saying as he did so that he was putting it on to crown him king. To Amasis what was done was not entirely unwelcome, as he showed by his behavior; for as soon as the rebellious Egyptians had set him up as king, he prepared to march against Apries. Apries, hearing this, sent one of his own attendants to Amasis, a man of reputation whose name was Patarbemis, ordering him to bring Amasis alive into his presence. When Patarbemis came and summoned Amasis, the latter, who happened to be sitting on horseback, lifted up his leg and behaved in an unseemly manner, telling him to take that back to Apries. Nevertheless, they say, Patarbemis pressed him to go to the king, since the king had sent to summon him, and he replied that for some time past he had been preparing to do so, and that Apries would have no cause to fault him. Then Patarbemis, perceiving his intent both from what he said and from seeing his preparations, departed in haste, wishing to inform the king as quickly as possible of what was going on. When he returned to Apries without bringing Amasis, the king, paying no attention to what he said, but moved by violent anger, ordered his ears and nose to be cut off. And the rest of the Egyptians who still remained on his side, when they saw the man of greatest reputation among them suffering such shameful outrage, waited no longer but joined the others in revolt and delivered themselves over to Amasis.

The man of reputation Apries sent to fetch Amasis back, and whose ears and nose Apries cut off when he came back without him — which lost Apries the rest of his subjects.

## modern-en · ladice · 396:0

Amasis also made a pact of friendship and alliance with the people of Cyrene. He decided to take a wife from there—either because he wanted a Greek wife, or simply out of friendship for Cyrene. He married a woman named Ladice, said by some to be the daughter of Battus, by others of Arcesilaus, and by still others of Critobulos, a prominent citizen. When Amasis lay with her, he found himself unable to consummate the marriage, though he had no trouble with his other wives. After this continued for some time, Amasis told Ladice he believed she had used witchcraft on him, and that nothing could save her from the worst death of any woman. Ladice denied everything, but Amasis was unmoved. So she silently vowed to Aphrodite that if Amasis lay with her successfully that night, she would send a statue to the goddess at Cyrene. Immediately after the vow, Amasis was able to perform. From then on, every time he came to her, he succeeded. He loved her very much after that. Ladice fulfilled her vow and sent the statue, which was still in good condition in my time, set up facing outward from the city of Cyrene. When Cambyses conquered Egypt and learned who Ladice was, he sent her home to Cyrene unharmed.

The Cyrenaean woman Amasis married, who prayed to Aphrodite when he could not come to her and afterwards sent the goddess a statue.

## modern-en · rhodopis · 349:0

This king also left behind him a pyramid, much smaller than his father's, square in shape and measuring three hundred feet lacking twenty on each side, built moreover of Ethiopian stone up to half its height. This pyramid some of the Greeks claim was built by the courtesan Rhodopis, but in saying this they are not speaking correctly. Besides, it is obvious to me that those who say this do not even know who Rhodopis was — otherwise they would not have attributed to her the building of a pyramid like this, on which, so to speak, countless thousands of talents were spent. Moreover, they do not know that Rhodopis flourished in the reign of Amasis, not in this king's reign, for Rhodopis lived many years later than the kings who left behind the pyramids. By descent she was Thracian, and she was a slave of Iadmon son of Hephaistopolis, a Samian, and a fellow-slave of Aesop the fable-maker — for he too was once the slave of Iadmon, as was proved especially by this fact: when the people of Delphi repeatedly proclaimed, in accordance with an oracle, that someone should claim the blood-money for Aesop's death, no one else came forward, but at length the grandson of Iadmon, also called Iadmon, claimed it; and so it is shown that Aesop too was Iadmon's slave.

The Thracian courtesan the Greeks credit with the third pyramid — wrongly, Herodotus says, since she lived generations later. She spent a tenth of her fortune on iron roasting-spits at Delphi.

## modern-en · charaxos · 350:0

As for Rhodopis, she came to Egypt brought by Xanthes the Samian, and having arrived there to practice her trade, she was ransomed from slavery for a large sum by a man of Mytilene, Charaxos son of Scamandronymos, the brother of Sappho the lyric poet. Thus Rhodopis was set free, and she remained in Egypt, and by her beauty she won so much favor that she made a great deal of money — great for someone like Rhodopis — though not enough to cover the cost of such a pyramid as this. In fact, there is no need to credit her with very great wealth, since the tithe of her wealth can still be seen even now by anyone who wants to look. For Rhodopis wished to leave behind in Hellas a memorial of herself — something that no one else had thought of or dedicated in a temple — and to offer it at Delphi as her memorial. Accordingly, with the tithe of her wealth she had iron spits made, large enough to pierce a whole ox, and many in number, going as far as her tithe allowed. She sent them to Delphi, and they are still lying there today, heaped together behind the altar the Chians dedicated, directly opposite the inner sanctum of the temple. As it happens, the courtesans at Naucratis tend to win renown, for this woman first, about whom this story is told, became so famous that every Greek without exception came to know the name of Rhodopis; and after her, one named Archidiche was sung about throughout Hellas, though she was less talked about than the former. As for Charaxos, after ransoming Rhodopis and returning to Mytilene, he was savagely abused by Sappho in an ode. About Rhodopis, then, I will say no more.

The man of Mytilene who bought Rhodopis’s freedom at great expense, and was mocked for it in his sister’s poetry.

And even supposing that for the first part of the time they had been so inclined, yet when many other Trojans besides were losing their lives as often as they fought with the Hellenes, and when of Priam's own sons two or three or even more were slain in every battle (if one may trust at all the Epic poets) — when, I say, things were coming to such a pass, I believe that even if Priam himself had had Helen as wife, he would have given her back to the Achaeans, if by so doing he might be freed from the evils that oppressed him. Nor was the kingdom coming to Alexander next, so that with Priam old the government was in his hands; but Hector, who was both older and more of a man than he, would have received it after Priam's death, and it would not have befitted Hector to allow his brother to continue his wrongdoing, seeing that great evils were coming to pass on his account both to himself privately and in general to the other Trojans. They told me he had come to Egypt for the reason the Hellenes also give — namely to bring the Gorgon's head from Libya — and had then visited them too and recognised all his kinsfolk; and they said he had thoroughly learnt the name of Chemmis before coming to Egypt, since he had heard it from his mother, and that they celebrated an athletic contest for him by his own command.

## modern-en · amphitryon · 258:0

About Heracles I heard the account that he was one of the twelve gods; but of the other Heracles whom the Hellenes know I was not able to hear anything in any part of Egypt. Moreover, to prove that the Egyptians did not take the name of Heracles from the Hellenes, but rather the Hellenes from the Egyptians — I mean those of the Hellenes who gave the name Heracles to the son of Amphitryon — of this, besides many other proofs, there is chiefly this: that the parents of this Heracles, Amphitryon and Alcmene, were both of Egyptian descent; and also that the Egyptians say they know neither the name of Poseidon nor of the Dioscuri, nor have these been accepted by them as gods among their other gods. Yet if they had received the name of any divinity from the Hellenes, they would naturally have preserved the memory of these most of all — assuming, as I suppose and as my judgment compels me to think, that in those times, as now, some of the Hellenes made voyages and were seafaring folk; so that the Egyptians would have learnt the names of these gods even more than that of Heracles. In fact, however, Heracles is a very ancient Egyptian god; and (as the Egyptians themselves say) it is seventeen thousand years to the beginning of the reign of Amasis from the time when the twelve gods — of whom they count Heracles one — were begotten of the eight gods.

Heracles’s mortal father — of Egyptian descent, the Egyptians say, which is why the Greeks are wrong about which Heracles is older.

Now I think that Melampus the son of Amytheon was not without knowledge of these rites of sacrifice, but was acquainted with them. For Melampus is the one who first set forth to the Hellenes the name of Dionysus and the manner of sacrifice and the procession of the phallos. Strictly speaking, when he made it known he did not take in the whole of it; but those wise men who came after him made it known more at large. Melampus, then, is the one who taught about the phallos that is carried in procession for Dionysus; and from him the Hellenes learnt to do what they do. I say, then, that Melampus, being a man of ability, devised for himself an art of divination, and having learnt from Egypt he taught the Hellenes many things, and among them those that concern Dionysus, making changes in some few points of them. For I shall not say that what is done in the worship of the god in Egypt came accidentally to be the same as what is done among the Hellenes, for then these rites would have been in character with the Hellenic worship and not lately brought in; nor indeed shall I say that the Egyptians took either this or any other customary observance from the Hellenes. But I think it most probable that Melampus learnt the matters concerning Dionysus from Cadmus the Tyrian and from those who came with him from Phoenicia to the land we now call Boeotia.

Son of Amytheon, who Herodotus thinks brought the rite of Dionysus into Greece from Egypt, having learned it from Cadmus and the Phoenicians.

These lines, when they reached him, pleased Croesus more than all the rest, for he supposed that a mule would never be ruler of the Medes in place of a man, and that consequently he himself and his heirs would never cease from their rule. On inquiring he found that the Lacedaemonians and the Athenians had the pre-eminence, the first among the Dorian and the others among the Ionian race. Now as to Heracles I have already shown how many years old he is according to the Egyptians themselves, reckoning down to the reign of Amasis; Pan is said to have existed even longer than these, while Dionysos is given the fewest years in comparison to the others, and even for him they count fifteen thousand years down to the reign of Amasis. ## modern-en · isis · 256:0

The clean males of the ox kind, then, both full-grown animals and calves, are sacrificed by all the Egyptians; but the females they may not sacrifice, for these are sacred to Isis. The figure of Isis is in the form of a woman with cow's horns, just as the Hellenes represent Io in pictures, and all the Egyptians without exception revere cows far more than any other kind of cattle. For this reason no Egyptian man or woman would kiss a Hellene on the mouth, nor will they use a knife, roasting-spits, or cauldron belonging to a Hellene, nor taste of the flesh even of a clean animal if it has been cut with a Hellene's knife. They bury the cattle of this kind that die in the following manner. The females they throw into the river, but the males they bury, each people in the outskirts of their town, with one of the horns (or sometimes both) protruding to mark the place. When the bodies have rotted away and the appointed time comes, then to each city comes a boat from what is called the island of Prosopitis (this is in the Delta, and the circuit of it measures nine schoeni). On this island of Prosopitis, besides many other cities, stands the one from which the boats come to collect the bones of the oxen; the city's name is Atarbechis, and in it there is a holy temple of Aphrodite. From this city many go out in various directions, some to one city and some to another, and when they have dug up the bones of the oxen they carry them off, and all together they bury them in a single place. In the same way they bury their other cattle when these die, for the same law is laid down concerning them, and these too they abstain from killing.

Now all who have a temple set up to the Theban Zeus, or who belong to the district of Thebes, sacrifice goats and abstain from sheep — for not all Egyptians equally reverence the same gods, except only Isis and Osiris (whom they say is Dionysus); these they all reverence alike. But those who have a temple of Mendes or belong to the Mendesian district abstain from goats and sacrifice sheep. The men of Thebes, and those who after their example abstain from sheep, say this custom was established among them for the following reason. Heracles (they say) had an earnest desire to see Zeus, and Zeus did not desire to be seen by him; at last, when Heracles was insistent in entreaty, Zeus devised this trick — he flayed a ram and held in front of him the head of the ram that he had cut off, and he put on over himself the fleece, and then showed himself to Heracles. Hence the Egyptians make the image of Zeus with the face of a ram; and the Ammonians do so also after their example, being settlers from both the Egyptians and the Ethiopians, and using a language that is a mixture of both tongues. And in my opinion it is from this god that the Ammonians took the name they bear, for the Egyptians call Zeus Amun. The Thebans, then, do not sacrifice rams but hold them sacred for this reason. Yet on one day of the year, at the feast of Zeus, they cut up and flay a single ram in the same manner, and cover the image of Zeus with its skin, and then they bring up to it another image of Heracles. How then should it flow from snow, when it flows from the hottest parts to those which are cooler? Indeed most of the facts are such as to convince any reasoning man that it is not at all likely it flows from snow. The first and greatest evidence is the winds, which blow hot from these regions; the second is that the land there is always rainless and without frost, whereas after snow has fallen rain must necessarily come within five days, so that if it snowed in those parts rain would fall there; the third evidence is the people dwelling there, who are black in colour because of the burning heat. Moreover, kites and swallows remain there throughout the year and do not leave the land; and cranes, fleeing the cold that sets in over Scythia, come regularly to these parts to winter. Etearchus said that once there had come to him men of the Nasamonians (this is a Libyan people who dwell in the Syrtis, and also in the land east of the Syrtis for no great distance), and when these Nasamonians came, and were asked by him whether they could tell him anything more than he knew about the desert parts of Libya, they said there had been among them certain sons of chief men, who were of unruly disposition; and these, when they grew up to be men, had devised various extravagant undertakings, and among them they drew lots for five of themselves to go and see the desert parts of Libya and try whether they could discover more than those who had previously explored furthest. For in the parts of Libya along the Northern Sea, beginning from Egypt and going as far as the headland of Soloeis (which is the extreme point of Libya), Libyans — and many races of them — extend along the whole coast, except such portions as the Hellenes and Phoenicians hold. But in the upper parts, which lie above the seacoast and above the peoples whose land comes down to the sea, Libya is full of wild beasts; and in the parts beyond the land of wild beasts it is full of sand, terribly waterless, and utterly desert. These young men then (they said), being sent out by their companions well supplied with water and provisions, went first through the inhabited country; after they had passed through this, they came to the country of wild beasts; and after this they passed through the desert, making their way towards the West Wind. Having crossed a great tract of sand in many days, they saw at last trees growing on a level place; and when they came up to them, they began to pluck the fruit that was on the trees. But as they began to pluck it, small men came upon them — of less stature than men of the common size — and these seized them and carried them off. Neither could the Nasamonians understand anything of their speech nor could those who were carrying them off understand the speech of the Nasamonians; and they led them (so it is said) through very great swamps, and after passing through these they came to a city in which all the men were of the same short stature as those who had carried them off, and black of skin. By the city ran a great river, which flowed from the west toward the sunrise, and in it were seen crocodiles.

If they really wished, as they claimed, to arrange the games justly, and if this was the reason they had come to Egypt, they advised them to arrange the contest so that only foreigners might compete in it, and no Eleian would be allowed to compete. Having this grievance, the Egyptian urged Cambyses on by advising him to ask Amasis for his daughter, so that Amasis would either be grieved if he gave her, or if he refused to give her, would offend Cambyses. Amasis, vexed and afraid of the power of the Persians, knew neither how to give nor how to refuse, for he was well aware that Cambyses meant to keep her not as a wife but as a concubine. Reckoning it this way, he did the following: there was a daughter of the former king Apries, very tall and of comely form, the only surviving member of his house, and her name was Nitetis. This girl Amasis adorned with fine clothing and gold, and sent off to Persia as his own daughter. But after a time, when Cambyses greeted her, calling her by the name of her father, the girl said to him: “O king, you do not realize how you have been deceived by Amasis; for he dressed me up in finery and sent me off, giving me to you as his own daughter, whereas in truth I am the daughter of Apries, against whom Amasis rose up along with the Egyptians and murdered him, though he was his lord and master.” These words, and the occasion that produced them, led Cambyses son of Cyrus against Egypt, moved to very great anger.

Apries’s daughter, whom Amasis sent to Cambyses in place of his own — and who told Cambyses whose daughter she really was. That, in the Egyptian telling, is why Persia invaded.

I was witness, moreover, to a great marvel, which the local inhabitants pointed out to me. Of the bones scattered about of those who fell in this fight — each side lying separately, since the bones of the Persians were heaped on one side, where they had been laid apart at the start, and those of the Egyptians on the other — the skulls of the Persians are so weak that if you hit them with just a pebble you will make a hole in them, while those of the Egyptians are so exceedingly strong that you would hardly break them by striking them with a large stone. The cause of this, they said — and I for my part readily believe them — is that the Egyptians from early childhood shave their heads, and the bone is thickened by exposure to the sun. This is also the reason why they do not become bald: for among the Egyptians you see fewer bald-headed men than among any other race. This, then, is why they have strong skulls. The reason the Persians have weak ones is that from infancy they keep their heads delicately in the shade by wearing tiaras, that is, felt caps. So much for that. I saw a similar thing at Papremis in the case of those who were slain along with Achaimenes son of Dareios, by Inaros the Libyan.

Darius’s son, killed with his army in Egypt by Inaros the Libyan — Herodotus looking forward out of his own narrative.

Now while Cambyses was marching against Egypt, the Lacedemonians had also made an expedition against Samos and against Polycrates son of Aiakes, who had risen up against the government and gained power over Samos. At first he had divided the state into three parts and given a share to his brothers Pantagnotos and Syloson; but afterwards he put one of them to death, and drove out the younger, Syloson, and so obtained possession of all Samos. Then, being in possession, he made a guest-friendship with Amasis king of Egypt, sending him gifts and receiving gifts in return. After this, within a short period, the power of Polycrates increased rapidly, and there was much fame of it not only in Ionia but also over the rest of Hellas: for wherever he directed his forces, everything went fortunately for him. He had gotten for himself a hundred fifty-oared galleys and a thousand archers, and he plundered all men indiscriminately, making no distinction; for he used to say that he would earn more gratitude from a friend by giving back what he had taken than by not taking at all. So he had conquered many of the islands and many cities on the mainland, and besides other things he won a sea-fight against the Lesbians as they were coming with their forces to aid the Milesians, and defeated them; and these men dug the whole trench round the wall of the city of Samos while working in chains.

## modern-en · eupalinos · 457:0

I have spoken at some length about the Samians because they have three works that are greater than any others ever constructed by Hellenes. First, a tunnel, open at both ends, dug through a mountain no less than one hundred and fifty fathoms high. The tunnel is seven furlongs long and eight feet high and wide, and throughout its whole length another channel has been cut twenty cubits deep and three feet wide, through which water is piped to the city from an abundant spring. The designer of this work was a Megarian, Eupalinos son of Naustrophos. That is one of the three. The second is a mole in the sea around the harbour, reaching down as much as twenty fathoms; its length is more than two furlongs. The third work they have accomplished is a temple larger than any other temple we know of. Its first designer was Rhoicos son of Philes, a native of Samos. For these reasons I have spoken at greater length of the Samians.

The Megarian engineer of the Samian tunnel, seven furlongs through a mountain and open at both ends — the first of the three greatest Greek works Herodotus knows.

## modern-en · oroetes · 517:0

Now about the time of Cambyses' illness, this had come to pass. There was a certain Oroetes, a Persian, whom Cyrus had appointed governor of the province of Sardis. This man had set his heart on an unholy thing. Though he had never suffered any wrong from Polycrates the Samian, nor heard a single offensive word from him, nor even seen him, he desired to seize him and put him to death, for a reason of this kind, as most who tell the story say. While Oroetes and another Persian named Mitrobates, governor of the province of Daskyleion, were sitting at the door of the king's court, they passed from words to a quarrel. As they disputed their respective claims to distinction, Mitrobates taunted Oroetes and said: “Do you count yourself a man? You have never yet won the island of Samos for the king, though it lies close to your province and is so extraordinarily easy to take that a native of it rose up against the government with fifteen men-at-arms, seized the island, and is now its despot.” Some say that because he heard this and was stung by the reproach, he conceived the desire not so much to take vengeance on the man who said it, as to destroy Polycrates at all costs, since it was on account of him that he was spoken of ill.

The Persian governor of Sardis who had Polycrates crucified out of nothing but pique at a slight he had imagined, and murdered Mitrobates and his son as well. Darius had him killed by a letter read out to his own guards.

## modern-en · bagaios · 525:0

Thus Darius asked, and thirty men undertook the task, each eager to do it himself. Darius stopped their contention and bade them cast lots. When they did so, Bagaios son of Artontes drew the lot out of them all. Having drawn the lot, Bagaios acted as follows: he wrote many papers dealing with various matters and set Darius' seal on them, and with these he went to Sardis. When he arrived there and came into Oroetes' presence, he took the covers off the papers one by one and gave them to the Royal Secretary to read—for all provincial governors have Royal Secretaries. Now Bagaios gave the papers in order to test the spearmen of the guard, to see whether they would accept the idea of revolting from Oroetes. When he saw that they paid great reverence to the papers and still greater reverence to the words read from them, he handed over another paper containing these words: “Persians, King Darius forbids you to serve as guards to Oroetes.” Hearing this, they lowered the points of their spears before him. Then Bagaios, seeing that they were obedient to the paper on this point, took courage and gave the last paper to the secretary. In it was written: “King Darius commands the Persians in Sardis to kill Oroetes.” So the spearmen of the guard, when they heard this, drew their swords and killed him on the spot. Thus retribution for the murder of Polycrates the Samian overtook Oroetes.

The son of Artontes who drew the lot, went to Sardis with a bundle of letters, and had Oroetes’s own bodyguard kill him by reading the last one aloud.

Now Periander had chosen out the sons of the leading men of Corcyra and was sending them to Sardis to be made eunuchs in order to take his revenge, since the Corcyreans had first begun the offense and had done him a deed of reckless wrong. For after Periander had killed his wife Melissa, it happened to him to experience another misfortune in addition to what had already happened, and it was this. He had by Melissa two sons, one seventeen and the other eighteen years old. Their mother's father Procles, who was despot of Epidauros, sent for these sons to visit him and entertained them kindly, as might be expected since they were the sons of his own daughter. Amasis became a friend of the Greeks. Among other tokens of friendship, he granted the city of Naucratis to Greeks who came to Egypt, giving them a place to live. For those who did not wish to settle but came on trading voyages, he set aside areas where they could erect altars and sacred precincts to their gods. The largest, most famous, and most used of these is called the Hellenion. It was founded jointly by the following cities: of the Ionians, Chios, Teos, Phocaea, and Clazomenae; of the Dorians, Rhodes, Cnidos, Halicarnassos, and Phaselis; of the Aeolians, Mytilene alone. The Hellenion belongs to these cities, and they are the ones who appoint the market supervisors. Other cities that claim a share have no right to one. She sent back word that she did not know, for she had never seen Smerdis son of Cyrus, nor did she know otherwise who the man was who lived with her. Otanes then sent a second time and said: “If you yourself do not know Smerdis son of Cyrus, then ask Atossa who this man is with whom both she and you live as wives. Now Darius had a clever groom whose name was Oibares. To this man, after they had left their assembly, Darius said: “Oibares, we have resolved about the kingship as follows: that the man whose horse neighs first at sunrise, when we are mounted, shall be king. So if you have any cleverness, contrive that we may win this prize, and no one else.” Oibares replied: “My master, if it truly depends on this whether you be king or not, take heart on this score and keep your courage high, for no other shall be king before you—such are the charms I have at my command.” Then Darius said: “If you have any such trick, now is the time to devise it and not to put it off, for our contest is tomorrow.” Oibares, hearing this, did as follows. As night was falling, he took one of the mares—the one which Darius' horse most preferred—and led her into the suburb of the city and tied her up. Then he brought up Darius' horse, led him around her for some time—bringing him so close that he touched the mare—and finally let the horse mount her.

Darius’s groom, who won him the kingdom before sunrise with a mare, a hand and a horse that neighed first.

To this Zopyros, son of Megabyzos, a prodigy occurred: one of the mules that served as bearers of provisions for him gave birth. Bearing in mind the words of the Babylonian who had said at the start that when mules bore young the wall would be taken—remembering, I say, this ominous saying—it seemed to Zopyros that Babylon could be taken. ## modern-en · indians · 435:0

It is clear to me, therefore, by every kind of proof, that Cambyses was exceedingly mad; for otherwise he would not have undertaken to mock religious rites and customary observances. For if one were to propose to all men a choice, bidding them select the best customs out of all the customs that exist, each race, after examining them all, would choose those of their own people; thus all think their own customs by far the best. And so it is unlikely that anyone but a madman would make jest of such things. That all men are accustomed to think this way about their customs, we may judge by many other proofs and especially by the following. Darius, in the course of his reign, summoned those of the Greeks who were present in his land and asked them for what price they would consent to eat the bodies of their fathers when they died; and they answered that for no price would they do so. After this Darius summoned those Indians who are called Callatians, who eat their parents, and asked them in the presence of the Greeks — who understood what was said by help of an interpreter — for what payment they would consent to burn the bodies of their fathers when they died; and they cried out loud and begged him to keep silence from such words. Thus, then, these things are established by custom, and I think Pindar spoke rightly in his verse when he said that “of all things, law is king.”

The most numerous nation Herodotus knows, whose Callatians eat their dead and who pay their tribute in gold dust.

On hearing the answer, he told the Spartan herald: "I have never yet feared the kind of men who have a special place in the center of their city where they gather to cheat each other with oaths." This was a jab at the Greeks for having marketplaces, something the Persians do not use—they never buy or sell in markets. He added: "If I stay healthy, it will be their own misfortunes they discuss, not those of the Ionians." Cyrus aimed this threat at all the Greeks, since they had marketplaces. He then appointed a Persian named Tabalos as governor of Sardis and gave a Lydian named Pactyas the task of transporting Croesus' gold. Babylon, the Bactrians, the Sacae, and the Egyptians—those were his primary concerns. He intended to lead campaigns against them himself and send a subordinate to handle the Ionians.

The list is Herodotus’s proof of what the empire actually was: not a conquest story but an accounts book.

## modern-en · targitaos · 562:0

Now the Scythians say their nation is the youngest of all peoples, and that this came about as follows. The first man ever to exist in this region, which was then desert, was one named Targitaos. Of this Targitaos they say—though I for my part do not believe it, but so they say—that his parents were Zeus and a daughter of the river Borysthenes. From some such origin as this, they report, Targitaos sprang, and from him were born three sons, Lipoxaïs, Arpoxaïs, and the youngest, Colaxaïs. In their reign there came down from heaven certain things wrought of gold—a plough, a yoke, a battle-axe, and a cup—and fell on the Scythian land. First the eldest saw them and came near, wanting to take them, but the gold blazed with fire at his approach. When he had gone away, the second approached, and again it did the same. So the gold repelled these two by blazing with fire. But when the third and youngest came up to it, the flame was quenched, and he carried the objects to his own house. The elder brothers, acknowledging the significance of the sign, handed the whole of the kingly power over to the youngest.

Aristeas, however, son of Caÿstrobios, a man of Proconnesos, said in the verses he composed that he came, possessed by Phoebus, to the land of the Issedonians, and that beyond the Issedonians dwelt the Arimaspians, a one-eyed race, and beyond them the gold-guarding griffins, and beyond them the Hyperboreans extending as far as the sea.
