Now the family of the Alcmaeonidae had already been prominent at Athens from the earliest times, and they became very greatly distinguished from the time of Alcmaeon and of Megacles after him. For Alcmaeon son of Megacles made himself of use to the Lydians sent from Croesus at Sardis to the oracle at Delphi, and assisted them energetically. When Croesus heard from the Lydians who had gone to the oracle that this man had served him well, he summoned him to Sardis, and when he arrived Croesus offered him as a gift as much gold as he could carry away on his own person at one time. With such a gift in view, Alcmaeon made preparations and resorted to these devices. He put on a large tunic, letting a deep fold of it hang open at the front, and he pulled on the widest boots he could find. So equipped he went into the treasury to which they led him. There he threw himself onto a heap of gold dust, and first he packed along the sides of his legs as much gold as his boots would hold; then he filled the whole fold of his tunic with gold and sprinkled some of the gold dust on his hair and took some into his mouth. Having done this, he came out of the treasury, dragging his boots with difficulty and looking like anything on earth except a man — for his mouth was stuffed full and every part of him was bulging. Croesus burst out laughing when he saw him, and not only gave him everything he was carrying but presented him with even more besides, of no less value. So this family became enormously wealthy, and this same Alcmaeon of whom I speak became a breeder of chariot horses and won a victory at Olympia.

Alcmaeon’s father, at the head of the Alcmaeonid line.

## modern-en · megacles-younger · 1017:0

That is how matters stood with the judgment of the suitors, and how the Alcmaeonidae became famous throughout Greece. From this marriage was born that Cleisthenes who established the tribes and the democracy for the Athenians — named after his maternal grandfather, the Sicyonian Cleisthenes. He was the son of Megacles; Megacles also had another son, Hippocrates, from whom came another Megacles and another Agariste, named after the Agariste who was daughter of Cleisthenes. This Agariste married Xanthippus son of Ariphron, and when she was pregnant she saw a dream in which it seemed to her that she had given birth to a lion. A few days later she bore to Xanthippus a son: Pericles.

Hippocrates’s son, a later Megacles of the same house.

## modern-en · aristonymus · 1012:0

Then in the next generation after this, Cleisthenes the tyrant of Sicyon raised the family still higher, so that it became much more famous among the Greeks than before. Cleisthenes son of Aristonymus, son of Myron, son of Andreas, had a daughter named Agariste, and he made it his purpose to find the best man in Greece and marry her to him. So when the Olympic games were being held and Cleisthenes won them with a four-horse chariot, he had it proclaimed that any Greek who considered himself worthy to be Cleisthenes's son-in-law should come to Sicyon by the sixtieth day, or sooner if he wished, for Cleisthenes meant to conclude the marriage within a year, counting from that sixtieth day. All those Greeks who took pride either in themselves or in their high birth came as suitors, and for them Cleisthenes had built a running-track and a wrestling-ground kept expressly for their use.

Cleisthenes of Sicyon’s father.

## modern-en · hippocleides · 1013:0

From Italy came Smindyrides son of Hippocrates of Sybaris, who of all men on earth had attained the highest degree of luxury (for Sybaris was at that time at the height of its prosperity), and Damasus of Siris, son of that Amyris who was called the Wise; these came from Italy. From the Ionian gulf came Amphimnestus son of Epistrophus of Epidamnus; from Aetolia came Males, the brother of that Titormus who surpassed all Greeks in strength and who fled the company of men to the remotest part of the Aetolian land. From the Peloponnese came Leocedes son of Pheidon the tyrant of the Argives — the Pheidon who established the standard weights and measures still used in the Peloponnese, and who outdid all other Greeks in outrageous arrogance, for he removed the Elean presidents of the games from their posts and presided over the Olympic games himself; I say, his son, and with him Amiantus son of Lycurgus, an Arcadian from Trapezus; and Laphanes, an Azanian from the city of Paios, the son of that Euphorion who, according to the Arcadian story, entertained the Dioscuri in his home and from then on made a point of welcoming everyone who came; and Onomastus son of Agaios of Elis — these came from the Peloponnese itself. From Athens came Megacles, son of that Alcmaeon who had gone to Croesus, and with him Hippocleides son of Tisander, who surpassed the other Athenians in both wealth and good looks. From Eretria, which was then flourishing, came Lysanias, alone from Euboea. From Thessaly came Diactorides of Crannon, a member of the Scopad family; and from the Molossians, Alcon.

The suitor Cleisthenes liked best, for himself and for his Corinthian connection — until he called for a table, danced Laconian figures and Attic figures on it, and then stood on his head and waved his legs. Told he had danced his marriage away, he said that Hippocleides did not care.

From Eretria, which was then flourishing, came Lysanias, alone from Euboea. From Thessaly came Diactorides of Crannon, a member of the Scopad family; and from the Molossians, Alcon.

Amiantus’s father. Neither the Spartan lawgiver nor the Athenian faction leader.

## modern-en · molossians · 145:0

For this reason, then, the Ionians also made twelve cities for themselves; for to say that these are in any way more Ionian than the other Ionians, or have a nobler descent, is mere folly. A large part of them are Abantians from Euboea, who have no share even in the name of Ionia; Minyai of Orchomenos have been mingled with them; also Cadmeians, Dryopians, Phokians who seceded from their native state, Molossians, Pelasgians of Arcadia, Dorians of Epidauros, and many other races have been mingled with them. And those of them who set forth to their settlements from the City Hall of Athens, and who consider themselves the most nobly born of the Ionians — these, I say, brought no women with them to their settlement, but took Carian women, whose parents they slew. On account of this slaughter, these women laid down a rule for themselves, imposing oaths on one another and handing it down to their daughters, that they should never eat with their husbands, nor should a wife call her own husband by name. This was because the Ionians had slain their fathers and husbands and children, and then, having done this, had taken them as wives. This happened at Miletos.

The people Alcon came from.

## modern-en · lysagoras · 1019:0

Having taken command of the force, Miltiades sailed against Paros, under the pretext that the Parians had first attacked Athens by sending triremes to Marathon along with the Persians — this was the excuse he put forward publicly, but he also had a private grudge against the Parians on account of Lysagoras son of Tisias, a Parian by birth, who had denounced him to Hydarnes the Persian. So when Miltiades arrived at his destination, he laid siege to the Parians with his army, first shutting them up within their walls; and sending a herald in to them he demanded one hundred talents, saying that if they refused to pay, his army would not withdraw until it had conquered them completely. The Parians had no intention of giving Miltiades any money; they thought only of how they might defend their city, and among many other contrivances they adopted this one: wherever at any point the wall was exposed to attack, they raised it to double its height under cover of night.

The Parian who denounced Miltiades to Hydarnes the Persian, and so gave him a private grudge against Paros to go with the public one.

## modern-en · timo · 1020:0

So much of the story is told by all the Greeks; but what followed the Parians alone report, and they say it happened like this. Miltiades, they say, was at a loss, when a woman came to speak with him, a Parian by birth named Timo who had been taken prisoner; she was an under-priestess of the chthonic goddesses. Coming into Miltiades's presence, she advised him that if it was of great importance to him to take Paros, he should do what she was about to suggest, and then she told him her meaning. So he crossed over to the hill that lies in front of the city and leapt over the fence of the temple of Demeter the Lawgiver, since he could not open the door; and having got over the fence, he went on towards the inner sanctuary, intending to do something inside — whether to lay hands on something that should not be touched, or whatever else he had in mind. When he reached the door, a sudden shuddering dread came over him and he set off to go back the way he had come; and as he leapt down from the wall of rough stones, his thigh was dislocated, or, as others say, he struck his knee against the wall.

The Parian under-priestess of the chthonic goddesses, a prisoner, who told Miltiades what to do to take Paros. The Parians wanted to kill her for it; the Pythia would not allow it, since Timo was not the author of the business but the means by which a man fated to end badly was led to his end.

## modern-en · thoas · 1024:0

These Pelasgians, now dwelling on Lemnos, wanted to get revenge on the Athenians. Having full knowledge of the Athenian festivals, they fitted out fifty-oared galleys and lay in wait for the Athenian women while they were celebrating a festival of Artemis at Brauron. They seized a number of them, sailed off, and carried them to Lemnos, where they kept them as concubines. When these women gradually bore more and more children, they took pains to teach their sons both the Attic language and Athenian manners. The boys would not mix with the sons of the Pelasgian wives, and if any one of them was struck by one of those other boys, they all came in a body to his defense; moreover, they claimed authority over the other boys and had the better of them with ease. The Pelasgians, observing this, took counsel, and a fear came over them: if these boys were already showing themselves resolved to stand together against the sons of the lawful wives, and were already trying to assert authority over them from the start, what would they do when they grew up to be men? So they decided to kill the sons of the Athenian women, and this they did; and they killed their mothers as well. From this deed, and from what was done before — when the Lemnian women killed their husbands, Thoas and the rest — it has become a custom throughout Greece that any act of exceptional cruelty is called a “Lemnian deed.”

The one husband named of those the Lemnian women killed.

Those who voted between the two opinions, and who were men of consequence in the king's eyes, were: first, the despots of the Hellespontians—Daphnis of Abydos, Hippoclos of Lampsacos, Herophantos of Parion, Metrodoros of Proconnesos, Aristagoras of Kyzicos, and Ariston of Byzantion—these were those from the Hellespont. From Ionia, Strattis of Chios, Aiakes of Samos, Laodamas of Phocaia, and Histiaios of Miletos, whose opinion had been proposed against Miltiades'. Of the Aeolians, the only man of consequence present was Aristagoras of Kyme.

Those who voted between the two opinions, and who were men of consequence in the king's eyes, were: first, the despots of the Hellespontians—Daphnis of Abydos, Hippoclos of Lampsacos, Herophantos of Parion, Metrodoros of Proconnesos, Aristagoras of Kyzicos, and Ariston of Byzantion—these were those from the Hellespont. From Ionia, Strattis of Chios, Aiakes of Samos, Laodamas of Phocaia, and Histiaios of Miletos, whose opinion had been proposed against Miltiades'. Of the Aeolians, the only man of consequence present was Aristagoras of Kyme.

Tyrant of Phocaea, in the same roll.
